utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation that is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Neuner has some questions for you. Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Witness, your name a Baton Haxhiu?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, my name is Baton Haxhiu.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And you were born on the 24th of February, 1966, in Pristina in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And you are a journalist by profession?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiu, is it correct that you gave a statement in August 2001 to the investigators of the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And when you came here for the Milosevic trial in May 2002, you made some corrections to this statement?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes. There were some minor mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And after you did these corrections, you confirmed the corrections and the statement in front of a Registry officer and stated that both the statements are true and correct to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And before you came here today, earlier this week, we in the Prosecution -- we communicated your statement and your transcript of testimonies to you before you travelled to come here?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So you had an opportunity to read all this material before you came here today, is it?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And you testified on the 23rd of May, 2002, in the Milosevic trial?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And you testified a second time on the 8th of November, 2006, this time in the Milutinovic case?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So together does the corrected statement and both transcripts of testimony truly and accurately reflect what you would say if you gave your testimony orally before this court today?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, I'll say the same things today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm referring to the statements, this is the 92 bis package, 65 ter number 2478. I'm also referring to the testimony in the Milosevic case, which is 02479. As well as to the testimony in the Milutinovic case, 05053. And I would like to tender all three items.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Each of those will be received as three separate exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: These would be Exhibits P992, P993, and P994, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I just wanted to make a clarification, in accordance with your decision on the 10th of February this year, the Prosecution has redacted parts of the statement and of the testimony of Mr. Haxhiu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And these are the parts relating to the meeting, and I will ask Mr. Haxhiu a short while about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiu, I wanted to read out a summary for the Court and for the people listening to us, a summary of what you have testified and to what you have stated in your statement. Mr. Haxhiu is a journalist and the founding member of the newspaper Koha Ditore. His evidence relates to the buildup of the conflict in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999. He describes that the conflict in Kosovo was closely linked to the issue using the Albanian language in university. In 1991, the Serbian government forced a more Serbian oriented curriculum in Kosovo schools. The parallel Albanian school system developed. The Serbian state did not recognise the diplomas. This led to non-violent student demonstrations. Baton Haxhiu was present and translated at meetings between Ambassador Petritsch, Jan Kickert, and Albert Rohan with KLA members in the summer of 1998. On the 2nd of October, 1998, the police broke into the offices of Koha Ditore and beat the witness and some of his colleagues. The witness was arrested and interrogated by the police. On 5 or 6 December, 1998, Stanisic stated at a meeting that Sreten Lukic had convinced Milosevic to break up the demonstration by force. Stanisic stated he could not decide anything on his own and that the proposal for a Kosovo republic would not be accepted. Such a proposal would not be acceptable to the nationalistic circle around Milosevic. Stanisic said that he would meet Milosevic the following day. Baton Haxhiu was in Pristina in March 1999. Leaving the town, he saw men in green uniforms wearing masks. The witness's father was beaten up in the streets of Pristina. Mr. Baton Haxhiu saw thousands of people in Pristina being expelled the day he left. He travelled through the mountains to the Macedonian border. There he saw more than 15 kilometres long line of refugees trying to cross into Macedonia. Baton Haxhiu reached Tetovo on the 7th of April, 1999. This witness's evidence is relevant to paragraphs 26, 72(g), 77, 80 to 102 of the indictment and counts 1, 2, and 5 of this indictment. End of the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm going to put now a few questions, Mr. Haxhiu, to you, relating to two topics. The first topic is a meeting at Mr. Bakalli's apartment. And my first question would be when about did this meeting at Mr. Bakalli's apartment take place?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: This meeting took place on the 13th or 14th of November. I had it written somewhere in a notebook, but I don't have it now. But I believe it was either the 14th -- 13th or 14th, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. And how was this meeting initiated?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: When I was arrested on the 2nd of October, I was interrogated for two and a half hours. And since it was an atmosphere of conflict and a war situation, I said that the best thing would be to stop the conflict and have the Albanians and the Serbs meet in order to talk on how to find a way out of this crisis and conflict situation. I indicated to them that you have the example of Bosnia and Croatia which would be the best way why we shouldn't use hard-line regarding the Kosova situation. And that was how this initiative emerged. Later, I received a phone call by Mr. Stijovic; I think it was the 13th of November when I got that phone call, 1997. And that was how the meeting was organised in the office of Mr. Bakalli.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Two questions. First of all, you said you were arrested on the 2nd of October. Which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you mentioned a gentleman, Mr. Stijovic. Could you explain to the Court who was Mr. Stijovic and what position did he hold in November 1997 when he called you?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: To my recollection, Stijovic used to be chairman of the youth -- socialist youth league of Prishtina, a Serb citizen who was in good relations with Albanians in normal circumstances. But I didn't know that Zoran Stijovic was a high-ranking official of the Serbian state and its service until the moment when I received his phone call.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Court what you mean by he "was a high-ranking official of the Serbian state and its service." Which service are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: In the meeting we were having in Bakalli's office, I realised that that person was a high-ranking official in the secret service because he was in the company of two main persons, officials, Mr. Hadjic and Mr. Gajic. In that meeting, I knew that Mr. Gajic was working there, but I didn't know that that was his true name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I take it one by one. You said you didn't know that Mr. Gajic was working there. Where was Mr. Gajic working in November 1997?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic was chief responsible for security issues, or as we call it in our daily speech, he was chief of secret service for Kosova. And he was in Kosova for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. Then you mentioned a second -- or another gentleman next to Mr. Gajic, could you give us the name of this person, could you spell it?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I don't know his name, but he introduced himself as Mr. Hadjic and as the assistance of Mr. Jovica Stankovic [as interpreted]. During the meeting he said that soon he would replace Mr. Gajic and that he would come in to Prishtina. That was what he stated at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So what did you conclude for which service if any was Mr. Hadjic working?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Because he was probably the main person, the key figure of the secret service of Serbia then --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: -- or Yugoslavia. He was the main figure after Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And can you give us the full name of Mr. Stanisic, please?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic in November 1997, what office, if any, was he holding?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: He was chief of Yugoslavian Secret Service. I think they had just changed the name at that time and I don't recall the exact nomination of that service.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us that secret service and Mr. Jovica Stanisic, to which minister, if any, did Mr. Stanisic report to?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I don't know. But the way I perceived it as a journalist, he had direct links with Milosevic. At least he didn't mention or refer to any minister with whom he had links or connections or to whom he reported. At least that was my impression from the meeting we had in 1997, which was the only meeting actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you, the three gentlemen did come to Mr. Bakalli's apartment for this meeting. Did they say on whose behalf they were coming? Or whom they represented at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: They came there on behalf of their chief and said that even Mr. Milosevic was informed of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And who was their chief?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I would presume that the chief would be Mr. Stanisic. Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you what, in one sentence, was the Albanian position promoted at the meeting in Mr. Bakalli's apartment?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: We knew that Serbia was a strong state and that it had a strong army and that it was impossible politically to deal with it. Therefore, since Yugoslavia was being demolished, was in a process of disintegration, that's why we proposed the establishment of an independent republic in an eventual confederation including Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do I understand correctly that the proposal was to have an independent republic of Kosovo but within the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: It was a confederation. I wouldn't describe it as Yugoslav confederation. We proposed that the name be changed. We proposed a confederation comprising Montenegro and Serbia because they formed the rest of former Yugoslavia, or they constituted the artificial patrimony to the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges what position Mr. Bakalli was holding at the time he was engaging in these proposals in November 1997?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: The movement of Albanians of Kosova didn't have positions or pass. In fact, we all -- Bakalli had a very strong political background. He was one of the key figures in the former Yugoslavia, and the man who in real terms established or built the concept of the former state that Milosevic and others inherited. He was the man who knew better than anyone the Serb mentality, better than anyone the Serbian political figures, better than anyone he knew what was called the political rear of Serbia because he had during that time built that concept for Kosova. He was one of the main persons in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Did he told an office in November 1997?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: There were, as I said, no offices or posts in Kosova because people were dismissed or laid off from their work, jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So you tell us that a proposal was promoted at the meeting by the Albanian side. Can you explain to the Court what the Serb reaction to that proposal was?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: The Serb reaction was furious. It was down-right refusal of that proposal. Their immediate response was this proposal will lead to war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Who said so, that it would lead to war?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Both, Gajic and Hadjic. The first to say it was Hadjic. Gajic simply nodded, confirmed it, what Hadjic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: What else was responded to that proposal?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: It was a lengthy meeting which lasted about three hours, but the most important part of that meeting, I would say, was the threats we received up to blackmail from our interlocutors. At the moment it was said that, Do you know that there are 443 ethnically pure villages in Kosova? We said, Yes, we know and then what. They said, You know that these -- the population of these villages can be driven out of these villages within 24 hours given the strength of Serbia. We said, Yes, we think it can be done but it would mark the end, if you like, to a concept of peace or peaceful concept. And this would lead to a constant war. And they promptly said, Have you heard of the project scorched earth?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'll stop you here for a second. Before we come to scorched earth, I want to clarify. These 443 ethnical pure villages in Kosovo referred to by these three gentlemen, which ethnicity was living in these 443 villages, Albanians or Serbs or others, could you clarify? How did you understand it?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, it was the first time for me to hear that there are 443 villages in Kosova inhabited by Albanians. They didn't refer to them as villages, they referred to them as settlements. So that was when I learned the number of villages, and that they had a very clear idea of what Kosova was like, how it functioned, and how many Albanians lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So they envisaged Albanian villages in Kosovo, and then you mentioned scorched earth. Could you explain what was said by the gentlemen in relation to scorched earth at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: As I said earlier, they referred to them as settlements. They knew what they meant by that word. And it was also the first time for me to hear the concept of scorched earth. I was young then, and I hadn't any idea of such conflicts of such genocidal dimension. The very -- the mere fact of using these words scorched land or earth was shocking to me. But for Bakalli, this was not new, he had already heard of it. And by this concept, this scorched land or earth, as they put it, it was a military police project which was in place ready to be activated at any moment, and for me this seemed the greatest threat. It was frightening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you remember who from these three gentlemen was mentioning the scorched earth concept?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Hadjic, but the others seemed to be familiar with that. So the conversation about the scorched earth went on for a couple of minutes. The two others didn't react, they were well aware of what it meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And they were well aware but did they oppose at some point in time the concept of scorched earth? What was your impression?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No, no. They were discussing about it as if it was the most normal thing. As a military option that might be activated or put in place in case the Albanians failed to obey the instructions of Serbia. They were clear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: What was the reaction by the Albanian side to the mentioning of scorched earth concept?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: There was nothing to be said other than, You are not the only ones living on this planet. And that the international community would certainly react to it because we are at the dawn of the 21st century, and you cannot come up with such concepts. Even if you were the only one living in this world, the implementation of such a project would be hard let alone that we are living in a world where there is an international law, where there are so many media outlets, and where it won't be easy for you to act. And they said, We will see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Did this response lead to more moderate response from the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No. Immediately after this they said to us, This is our mandate, we cannot elaborate any more on this. We will go back to Belgrade and present the Belgrade officials with our impressions. They said that it would be possible for us to meet Milosevic. We refused that. And then they said that there is a likelihood for another meeting between us to be held. And that's how this meeting was concluded that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Was there, following this meeting in the apartment of Mr. Bakalli, another meeting, a follow-up meeting?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: With these gentlemen you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: With these gentlemen or with any Serbian representative who wanted to speak to Mr. Bakalli or you?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: The following meeting was held sometime in December. I don't know the exact date. It was a meeting with Mr. Jovica Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And you say the meeting was in December, which year, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: At this meeting with Mr. Stanisic, was the concept of scorched earth mentioned?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No. Stanisic had come there with a political stance. He was presenting surprising offers to us, surprising in a sense that we knew that we were not going to accept them. He had a stronger mandate than the people from the previous group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us briefly what the surprise was, or the surprising offer?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: He offered Bakalli the post of Yugoslavia's vice-president. To my knowledge, Yugoslavia was not functioning at the time, so this post didn't make any sense. But Bakalli replied by saying that he has finished with his mandate in former Yugoslavia and that his efforts were towards finding solution to the problem of Kosova the way he had put the proposals forward to the Serb party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: In terms of threats for violence, as one may interpret the mentioning of scorched earth at the previous meeting, at the follow-up meeting, was there any threat about violence mentioned?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Stanisic used another language, a language of sophisticated threats. It wasn't a brutal language that the others used. He said that there were many nationalists and radicals around Milosevic that would never accept our proposal, and he said, My friends - this is what he used, the word - we are going towards a war. My impression was that this person had gained experience from the previous wars in Bosnia and Croatia, and he wanted to win the battle; but it seemed that his mandate was also limited. He offered us to meet Milosevic, which we refused. Then he said to us that he was going to meet Mr. Milosevic the following morning to present him with our proposals, but he told us that he was sure Milosevic was not going to accept our proposals. To what I know, after this meeting and after several months, Mr. Stanisic was removed from the post he held. I'm not quite sure how long after this meeting he was removed, maybe a month or so. There was a public resignation on his part, and I'm trying to para-phrase it: All my responsibilities are dedicated to my boss and the president, Mr. Milosevic. I haven't done anything that has been, to my knowledge, ordered by him. This is, as far as I remember, the statement he gave when he resigned. This is a long time ago, but this is approximately what the wording was in that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you, I want to have a very brief answer to my following question. From the Serbian side, did you ever hear again the words scorched earth uttered in the following weeks and months?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Officially or publicly, never; but at meetings with colleagues, journalist, of course they were aware of this. The story of scorched earth or land became public later on in the end of 1998 or beginning of 1999; I don't know the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Am I right in putting to you that from an official representative of the Serb regime, you didn't hear scorched earth being uttered after the first meeting in Mr. Bakalli's apartment and the following months?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I want to move to my second topic. I want to leave it aside. I want to move to Pristina now, the events in March and early April 1999. Mr. Bakalli [sic] -- Mr. Haxhiu, excuse me, you lived in Pristina all your life, did you?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And in early March 1999, where did you live?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I was living in Kodra e Diellit neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter number 13 being displayed to this witness, please. Or actually, I have a hard copy. Maybe it's easier, because I want to introduce a document, to show him the hard copy on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Page 14, line 1 should read "that has not been, to his knowledge, or ordered by him."

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: First of all, I wanted -- we don't have an image yet. Okay. Sorry, it's on e-court. The best would be actually if we use the ELMO image because I want to later on introduce through e-court another document. Can we zoom out a little bit because -- if I can ask the usher to zoom out a little bit, yeah. And turn the map a little bit around, right now it lies -- not upside down. Could we just turn the map, rotate the map a little bit. Yes. Thank you. Yes, perfect. And zoom out a little bit so that the Judges can see everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: First I would like to ask you. If it is displayed here - and Mr. Haxhiu, please look at the ELMO next to you, to your right-hand side. Could I ask you to encircle, if you find it, the place or the apartment of Mr. Bakalli was, or the meeting in November 1997.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: It should be somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes, you've encircled a building. Can you mark a number 1 below it or somewhere. Yes. I can't read this number 1, can you make the number 1 below the circle maybe, or somewhere where there is a white --

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Below the circle, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Then I wanted to ask you, where were you living in March 1999? You mentioned in Kodra e Diellit?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: This part here should be Kodra e Diellit. This part here is the whole Kodra e Diellit neighbourhood, and I should be here somewhere, that is my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You marked a number 2 next to the circle, which you've drawn. Can you tell us the security situation in March 1999? How did it develop in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: From October 1998 up until the 23rd of March, 1999, the situation was tense with concentration of police forces, Arkan forces, and paramilitary forces in uniforms. They were present in the whole territory of Kosova, especially in Prishtina. I'm talking about the time-frame when Mr. Holbrooke and Mr. Milosevic were trying to reach an agreement to end the crisis in Kosova. I'm talking about the period of the October or so agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. Taking you to Pristina, and I'm only asking you now about Pristina. Can you tell us, once the NATO air-strikes had started on the 24th of March, 1999, how did the security situation in Pristina develop?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: When the Rambouillet talks failed on the 21st, we have the first real killing in the town. Arianit Kelmendi was killed and another person was wounded. Forces started to shoot at facilities. These were not police forces; these were other people who had been armed in the meantime and who were walking and driving around freely in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can I stop you here for a second, because I want to clarify a few things of what you said. You say on the 21st Kelmendi was killed. Which month and year are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: That is 21st of March, 1999. Life in Prishtina at this time would end at 5 p.m. People were trying to avoid being on the streets after 5.00. Everybody would stay at home with the exception of Serbs, of course. Personally, as I had to work in the newspaper, I had to finish all my work earlier in late afternoon instead of doing it as usually in the evening. People who were working in the printing house, they would remain there the whole night because they were scared to go out in the dark because darkness was a synonym of killings, of fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can I ask you again about Mr. Kelmendi. You said he was killed on the 21st of March, 1999. What role, if any, did Mr. Kelmendi have, at that time?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: We are talking about Arianit Kelmendi who was killed on the 21st of March, he was a waiter, a civilian, who was killed in front of the cafe where he was working. This happened on the 21st, three days prior to the bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know anything about the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: The power to instate fear and to draft such actions came from the Serbs --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. But --

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: -- from the Serbian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: -- in fact, you don't know who perpetrated this crime?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. After the 24th of March, 1999, you mention here on your map that you were generally living at the house you encircled as number 2 on the map. Did you stay to live at that house after the beginning of the air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No, I didn't. A friend of mine, a British diplomat, suggested to me that it would be better that I didn't spend the night in my own house. On the first night of the bombing, I slept in a house somewhere in the centre of the town. We were told that the centre of the town was always safer during the bombing because it was very difficult to bomb it. So we were advised to avoid the peripheral areas, because it was more dangerous for us to stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So you then stayed in the centre of the town. Did you stay there until you left Pristina, or could you explain?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No. I honestly didn't expect that it would be that terrifying immediately after the first night of the bombing. We could see through the window terrible things out there. I spent that night there, and the following morning at 9.00, I had organised a meeting with a journalist of Koha e Ditore; but when I arrived there, the guard of Koha Ditore was killed, all the computers were stolen, everything was emptied, and there I saw uniformed policemen. I asked him, Who was killed here? And they replied, Unidentified forces killed a person who was guarding this company. And that same night, the printing shop of our newspaper was burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can I ask you for --

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I just wanted to say that the bombing would lead to peaceful negotiations shortly after. We didn't expect at all that this would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to go back to what happened to your newspaper and its staff. Could you give us the name of the guard who was killed?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: We refer to him with another name, uncle something, but I don't remember his name right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you know his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: He was an Albanian, 57 or 58 years old. He had been working with Koha Ditore as a guard from the time it was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Then you mentioned here: "I asked, Who was killed here? And they replied, Unidentified forces killed a person who was guarding this company." Can you tell me, who replied to you?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: There were policemen right at the entrance. They smelled of rakija of alcohol. I guess they had finished up the alcohol we had in our office for special occasions. I could see traces of blood. I guess they had dragged the body of the guard; and I could see the traces of blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. First of all, looking at this map again, could you encircle the building where Koha Ditore was and where this killing occurred, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can we a better marker for the witness? Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And you marked a number 3 next to this. Thank you. To help us, on what day did the crime of killing the guard and the destruction or looting of the premises of Koha Ditore occur?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: That would be between the 24th and 25th of March, sometime after midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. Then you mentioned that you were moving around a little bit. First you were in a house in the centre and then you moved further. Could you, by marking the location in the centre with number 4, say where you were first, after the war started?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: This stall building here should be the one. I will mark it with 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And when did you leave that location to live somewhere else in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: On the 27th. I spent two days there and returned to Kodra e Diellit on the 27th, I think, though I cannot be accurate. I returned to Kodra e Diellit here somewhere in this part at about 250 metres away from my home. I was staying with a friend of mine, a writer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You marked this location with a number 5. When did you leave, finally, that location to go and leave the town? I understand from your testimony.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: This should be between the 29th, and I didn't leave but we were staying in a basement. During the day we would stay in the apartment, and during nights we would stay in basements because darkness was dangerous. On the 29th, I saw for the first time armed forces masked with green overalls. This was the first time I saw numbers forces dressed in green overalls. They were in the company of local policemen who were familiar with the terrain and knew exactly who was what and which part of the town was where. So these forces were in the company of a smaller group of local policemen. The policemen were not wearing masks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And can you describe the uniforms worn by these policemen?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: It was kind of a unique uniform. An overall, not on buttons, but with a zipper from here to here. Then there was the green mask; you could only see the eyes. And they moved in two lines. And at the end of each line there were uniformed policemen. And they would usually stay 10 metres or so behind the people they were expelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. The overall was worn by policemen or was worn by the paramilitaries? I'm a little bit unclear, I just want to clarify.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No, the policemen were wearing police uniforms, but they were few in numbers. Whereas these other forces were wearing automatic -- another form of automatic rifle. They were stouter. They were not of the appearance of the usual police. They had round potted bellies. Not the usual police, you know, figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: They had green overall -- they had green uniforms or whatever, yeah?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, one solid colour green.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. But I was asking you for the dress worn by the policemen who were a few metres behind. Can you describe why you believe these persons were policemen?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: These persons were wearing blue uniforms, but in that case they were wearing shirts, blue shirts, and a jacket. The usual police uniforms you could see in police patrols in the city. They were escorting these other forces that I mentioned wearing green uniform, but they weren't giving any orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. What I'm interested in is looking at the clothes for a second again. Are we talking about plain or camouflage police uniforms? Are we talking -- about which colour are we talking?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: We are talking of the usual police uniform that is one colour, solid colour. Not camouflage. But I think they were very few in numbers, maybe five.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Which is the colour of the uniform they had, the plain uniform?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Dark blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to show you now one document and then conclude. I'm still leaving the map on the screen because I will use it in a moment again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can we have, please, 65 ter number 407 on our screens, and I need the second page right away, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: For your information, these are excerpts which have been taken out of the so-called Blue Book from the Kosovo Verification Mission of the OSCE and they all relate to Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I may have given the wrong 65 ter number. It is 041 -- sorry, 0407.01. This is the wrong item here on our screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence will object to this whole discussion about this evidence. First of all, we don't have the source of the information presented in that book. Rather, there are some numbers such as C08, C25, and so on and so forth. But I think one might even debate the format of this Blue Book; therefore, we will be lodging an objection in terms of this being admitted into evidence at this point, unless, of course, the OTP can reveal the source of their information to us which in turn might effect our own position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware about this point, and all I can say is that a witness who is coming next week, I don't know his exact name, I think Drewienkiewicz.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: DZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: General DZ, yes. He is in a perfect position to explain how the information was assembled and put together. All I wanted to do now is to show this witness some of the information gathered in the time-period in which this witness was in Pristina. And since he was also moving around, I thought that he may be in a position to confirm or dismiss some of the information or make a general comments and add some of his own observations to it. I'm not -- I'm not intending to have this witness giving any background about how this document was produced and so on. This would be General Drewienkiewicz who is coming next week who could explain that in more detail, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologize. Just very briefly, Your Honours. I do believe that my learned friend Mr. Neuner could ask his questions in relation to any information he wishes to retrieve from the witness. Subjects that have not been raised in the statement or in the witness's testimony before this Tribunal, if he can obtain that from the witness then he doesn't even have to do what he has been trying to do. Nevertheless, I gave you my reasons, and I think they are valid reasons when it comes to documents such adds these when sources are specifically stated. Secondly, we are not sure about General Drewienkiewicz - I think that's his real name - and he should be one of the next witnesses to appear here in this court, that he will be able to confirm many things before this Tribunal in terms of the source of the information in relation to the documents that my learned friend has every intention of sharing to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner, what you propose is not altogether clear to us, but presents some difficulties. It's one thing to have the witness describe what he saw and perhaps then have it confirmed that that's the same sort of thing that you find in this book. It's another thing for this witness to be shown the book and say whether he can say something like that occurred or not because that's clearly prompting the witness to speak of things rather than he working on his recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The book itself could not be admitted in evidence until such time as somebody can speak about it making and reliability. You anticipate that could be a witness next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes, there will be. Simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's not clear to us why you need to use the book at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I wanted to use the book because this witness was in Pristina himself and has moved around in this time-period after the war broke out and has made certain observations. And he has already stated to Your Honours that he saw, for example, that his own officers in Kodra Ditore had been looted. And in this Blue Book, there's such entries which refer to looting against the Albanian population or of businesses of the Albanian population. And I just wanted to show that to the witness to elicit whether he could confirm that or could dismiss it. I thought I'm first giving him an opportunity to state what he has observed, and after I laid this foundation that then the appropriate time has come to show him a few of these more abstract entries. One other entry also relates to the expulsion of the population from an area where this witness has lived and where he has indicated on the map that he was twice there in the relevant time-period from where he finally left Pristina to go to Tetovo, so there is a direct connection between the entries which I have selected and what the witness has personally experienced. Maybe as a -- because he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner, I think you are missing the point. Why is it that the witness is not able to simply describe what he saw, what he observed?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm prepared not to show the book and not to show the excerpts. An alternative could have been I'm showing him the excerpts and wait for the entire book to be tendered next week, so we have some comments now on the record. I don't need to mark it even for identification, the excerpt, I could, but I don't have to. I can also just go on, elicit a few more questions about what the witness experienced, and then leave it there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that might --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: It's an agreeable course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- be the best course --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- and we'll hear from the witness what he observed, what he understood, rather than him merely commenting on somebody else's book.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm, Your Honours, saying I will proceed as suggested. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiu, I wanted to ask you a little bit about when did you have to move from one place to another after the 24th of March, 1999, did you move during the day, or did you move at other times?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This should be removed from the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was my objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you now answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: At 9.30, after I found out about the murder of the guard of Koha Ditore seeing that the situation was risky, that the war was different from what we had thought about it, we left the centre. And as we were instructed, we -- not to stay in one place, we kept moving from one apartment to the other in Dardanija neighbourhood. On the 24th, we stayed until the 26th when again I left for Kodra e Diellit to my friend's house Taki Dervishi. So I stayed in Kodra e Diellit in another part from where my house was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Who was the reason that you adopted this, if I may call it, "policy" of not staying at one place but rather moving around constantly, staying at different places over night?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Between the 24th and 25th, my lawyer was killed, his name was Bajram Kelmendi, together with his sons, one under 18, and the other a grownup. Lawyer Bajram Kelmendi was my attorney in respect to an article in the newspaper on the -- a trial was held on the 21st, even though it was a Sunday, but that was how it was done then. The fact that he was killed and also the fact that our foreign diplomat friends advised us not to remain in one place made us move from one place to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. Can I first of all clarify, the 21st, you said, when the trial was. Are we talking about which month and year, please?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Three days before the bombing. It was in that extraordinary trial which was held on Sunday, I was sentenced to a fine of 300.000 dinars which was quite a huge amount of money then. I don't know what it would be like now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: For what crime or offence, if I may ask?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: For publishing an article in the newspaper, a communique or a normal communique. We had been publishing them regularly until then, which we received from the KLA. A communique was an official one, it was published also by the Serb media outlets. I think that was not the real reason, because we had been doing that for months. But that was a pretext in order to strike at us. And the trial was held at 4.00 in the afternoon of a Sunday. It was hard for them to find an interpreter, to find a Serb judge, to find the investigating judge, so they had it ready, the trial was ready to start at 4.00. And we had to remain in the court building all day, together with Bajram Kelmendi and the managing director, Luan Dubroshi.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So Mr. Kelmendi was defending you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you tell us in front of which court he was defending you?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: In the communal court of Prishtina, municipal court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And you say three days after that trial he was killed. Can you, by looking at the map next to you, indicate where the location of his killing was?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I know where he was -- a place where he was taken from, but I don't know exactly the place where he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Then if you could encircle the place where he was taken from, and mark a 6 next to this, please.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you learn about the perpetrators who did this?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: After many years now, it is a known fact who the perpetrators were. They were police and the secret service people who took him and killed him in the middle of the road. Now, in this place, there is a gas station, and there is also a monument erected to them at the exit of Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And why do you say it's a known fact that the police and secret service people did it?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Because this was certified also by the counsel for the protection of human rights and freedom, also the organisation led by Natasha Kandic in Belgrade, and his spouse who carried on a kind of investigation of the people who committed that crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Was there an official confirmation?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Of course there will never be any official confirmation, but researchers showed who the perpetrators were both for Mr. Agani and Kelmendi. Mr. Kelmendi was also --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Mr. Agani was also the drafter of the file for genocide against Mr. Milosevic and the Serbian state, which, I think, has been submitted also to the Tribunal here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, when was Mr. Agani killed?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Mr. Agani was killed in May, at the end of April or beginning of May 1999. He was made to get off the train towards Macedonia, was taken to a police station, and was killed -- was shot with two bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: But you yourself didn't see this, you have heard this?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No. At the time I was in Macedonia, and I went there about a month before he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: But it is a common fact that in the case of Agani it was acknowledged that his murder was something done by people who did not belong to an institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You say "it was acknowledged." Who acknowledged anything?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: It was acknowledged in a way, let's say, to his family, to the officials; and I believe that soon there will be a trial regarding that murder. But for the moment, there isn't any official statement on the murder. The name is not public knowledge, but people more or less -- there is a guess, not a guess but it's a fact who is known who murder is, but it's not acknowledged publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Was there an indictment issued already?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: There is an ongoing process underway because it is known who the murderer was now after so many years have passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So are you sure there was an indictment or not?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No, there isn't until this moment, but it exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to take you a little bit to the reasons why you finally left Pristina at the end of March 1999. Could you tell me, what was the main reason that you left your hiding place, if I may call it, at the end of March and proceeded with the car, as you have testified, to leave Pristina?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: In Kodra e Diellit neighbourhood, there are about 120.000 inhabitants and there are three parts in this neighbourhood. At least at that time there were three sections or parts in the neighbourhood because now it's become greater. At the end of this neighbourhood where there are white coloured buildings, the first deportation started. And when people were coming from the other parts, they came to the Kodra e Diellit -- to the centre of Kodra e Diellit or the middle part of it. There is a parking-lot, a large parking-lot there, and people were walking, and behind them were uniformed people, the ones I mentioned earlier, those wearing green uniforms. When they came to our buildings, they gave the order that within five minutes all the people, the inhabitants, should leave their apartments. And we went down and joined that large group of people. And they also ordered a policeman and one of those persons wearing green uniforms to see if there was any inhabitants left. After that, they also ordered that the people who owned cars should get their cars and leave in the direction of Macedonia. Those who didn't, should go in the direction of the train station in Fushe Kosova. And they allowed us to go in two different directions: to Macedonia and to Albania. On the road in every check-point there was an armoured car manned by soldiers who didn't allow us to go in another direction but only in the indicated direction until the main road leading towards Macedonia. Along the main road in every check-point there were also policemen and armoured cars and the road was checked up to the border with Macedonia, it was under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: A few final questions before we break. Did you see the persons who were ordering the building where you were at the time in Pristina, did you see these persons ordering that people had to leave? Did you hear them ordering?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: The policemen didn't speak, they simply were escorting us. This was one, a pot bellied one, who ordered in a loud voice -- gave this order in a loud voice that all people should leave their houses. And he was wearing a mask and he was wearing a uniform. I saw them with my own eyes because they were not far from where I was. You could see that their accent was not the usual Serb accent from Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The person you were just describing who has ordered, was he a policemen or was he rather a member of this green uniform group with masks?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: He was one of these green uniform group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Then you mentioned that everybody had to assemble at a parking-lot. Would you find the parking-lot here on your map which you have drawn?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No. They didn't give the order for us to gather to this parking-lot, but the people simply got there, assembled there, because it was a clean area, open area. Then they gave the order for us to leave either in cars or to walk. This must be the parking-lot that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. You've marked a number 7 next to the bigger circle. And then you were proceeding -- okay, first of all, how many people did you see at this parking-lot marked with number 7?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Many. There were many people. Maybe about 20.000. I couldn't give you an accurate figure. But while we were staying in that parking-lot, we saw people walking in a street higher up leaving the city. They had also been ordered to leave, and we could see them walking above us. But the convoy of cars was kilometres long. Many kilometres long.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Who gave the persons gathering at the parking-lot the order to move?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: The same person. He simply said, Leave now. That was all he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And along the way in Pristina, what was your impression -- who controlled the traffic that day at the end of March 1999 when you were leaving Pristina?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Inside the city there were police armoured vehicles. Outside the city there were military armoured vehicles and other vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Did you come across, leaving Pristina that day, any police check-points?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: All the cars were -- most of them were stopped by the policemen who were stationed all over the road at everyone check-point. There were police and soldiers. They were, for example, telling the cars that you could drive only 20, 30, kilometres per hour. And they stopped the cars and asked them about the money they had on them. And if they had 300 marks. In my case, I gave about 200 marks to them because I was with my -- with another family I got on the way, we were five of us in our car.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note the time, I would seek to tender that annotated map, 65 ter number 13. And then the Prosecution would have no further questions at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The map will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P995, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We must now have our first break. We will resume at 5 minutes past 11.00 to continue your evidence. A court officer will assist you on the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic has some questions for you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiu, good morning.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragoljub Djordjevic. I appear on behalf of the accused in this case. I will have some questions of you, as you were told by the presiding Judge, in order to try and clarify some important issues having to do with the events you testified to today as well as in some related cases. I will see to it that my examination develops in such a way so as to have it completed today in order for you not to have to stay until tomorrow. What is your formal educational background, Mr. Haxhiu? Which schools did you complete?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Faculty of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement from 2001 you said that you had a law degree and that at the state university that was your core subject in 1991; however, your diploma was issued by a parallel university in 1992. Am I correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to caution you about the breaks since we speak different languages.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Do you want me to speak Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No, you can go on in Albanian. I just wanted to warn you about the pauses that I make. Mr. Haxhiu, let's clear up another thing which was unclear from your statement. I believe it was paragraph 7 of your statement, both pages 2 and 3, wherein you say that the first diplomas of the parallel university were being issued in 1996 and 1997 for the first time to their students. You said that you received your law degree or law diploma in 1992 at the parallel university. Can you explain what it was all about since the first diplomas apparently were being issued as early as 1996?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: When I started my studies -- I started my studies in the public university, the state-owned university. And the regular lectures, I completed them in 1989. There were some exams to go through of the fourth year. After that, the so-called process of the breaking up of the Kosova education system started, and we were evicted, as it were, from the state system and we started the parallel university, and the parallel system. So there were a number of exams, outstanding exams, which were to be completed and were completed in the private parallel university. So the first degrees were issued in 1992. The first generation of students in the parallel system started in 1992. It was then called the parallel educational system in Kosova. That's the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, therefore, that the parallel university from which your degree comes, in a way honoured all of your exams previously taken at the state university, you only had to make up for the exams you never took, that is to say, the final year?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Because all the professorship and the administration, the Albanian stuff, moved to the administration of the parallel university.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiu, one other question on that topic. Since you studied at this state university, were you in a position to have your lectures in the Albanian language as well as to take exams in that same language? Were you entitled to that?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I was a regular student, and I took my exams in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From the numerous statements you gave, be it to the Tribunal or its investigators, I gathered that you understand and speak the English language very well. My question for you is, where did you learn the English language so well?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: At school where we were taught English, but we also -- we also had the books and tapes which I bought, part in Belgrade and part in Zagreb. That was an English teaching method. There were no Albanian textbooks for this purpose. There were different ways of learning English, but mainly we bought those books either in Belgrade or in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Based on everything I could see in your statements, I also concluded that while you were a journalist and activist fighting for the rights of the Albanian population in Kosovo, you frequently had contacts with diplomatic representatives. They were primarily focused on establishing liaison with the KLA. First of all, in the course of such contacts, were you known under a certain nickname or a code-name?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I don't know what you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I mean a nickname.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will explain why I asked you that. There is a mention of a journalist in international journalistic circles, his name was Lum or Liu Haxhiu. I wanted know whether that person might not be you?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No, no. Lum Haxhiu was a fighter of the KLA and has no connection to myself or my family. And he lived and still lives in the Ferizaj area. He has never been a journalist. He came from Switzerland, and he became a KLA fighter. I don't know what his name is. I can't remember his name at the moment, but as far as I know, if I'm not mistaken, he is an MP in the Kosova parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Since it is not the same person as you, then it no longer matters. My next question on the general topics is this: Did you participate together with Mr. Haradinaj in the founding of the Albanian movement in Macedonia called "Ana"?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Never, never in my life have I taken part in the foundation of any organisation. My only profession has been and is journalism. I've never been part of any political party or organisation and have never taken part in the formation of any organisation, not a single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm glad to have cleared that up, therefore I will no longer put questions to you in that regard. Mr. Haxhiu, you are a journalist, but you are also a fellow lawyer. I'm not going to ask you about law since obviously your life developed in a different direction, but I wanted to ask you something about your 2001 statement. Do you recall having given that statement to a certain gentleman by the name of Fred Abrahams, the other person was Jonathan Sutch they told you they were investigators of The Hague Tribunal. I refer to your 2001 statement.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, I gave the statement in my house for only one reason because I trusted Fred Abrahams because I knew him before and I've known him for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: He was there as an investigator of this Tribunal, although you are telling us that you had known him from before. Can you explain to us the background of your relationship, of your acquaintance with Mr. Abrahams?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: In fact, as an investigator, it was Mr. Sutch who presented himself as an investigator. I knew Fred Abrahams for years from his activity in the Balkans. He was a representative of Human Rights Watch starting from 1994/1995 when I first knew him during his visit to Prishtina. Whenever he came to Prishtina, he was a guest of the Koha company.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you provided that statement in your house; is that correct? In 2001?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes. We established contact in my office, but then we -- I gave my statement in the calm of my own house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall, the interview was, A, tape recorded, and, B, conducted in English; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In the days following the day of your statement, the witness was brought -- the statement was brought back to you for you to review it and sign it. Who brought it to you?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: The statement was recorded, then it was transcribed; and I read the transcript, and I confirmed that it was my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Briefly we'll have to go back to 1991 since you referred to that year on a number of occasions in your statements. You also mentioned the fact that the Serb authorities abolished all Albanian language instruction. This is a general assertion that one comes across in several of your statements, eventually leading in different directions. My question is this: 1991 was the year following the new Serbian constitution which was passed in 1990. The constitution mentions the use of minority languages, but that year and in the years preceding that, a law was passed on the official use of language. There were also laws on the elementary, secondary, and higher degree education, which also partially referred to the rights of the minorities living in the territory of the FRY and Serbia, as well as the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija, as it is called, in the 1990 constitution. Having in mind all of those legal documents, would you agree with me that the use of minority languages is allowed in education, if you can answer that question of mine? If so, perhaps I can put an additional question right away, since I can see that you are following quite well what I'm saying, and it directly relates to the first question. It has to do with the curricula in use in the educational system. Was the curriculum the basic point of contention between the Serbs and Albanians in your view?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: One sentence I'd like to answer, the whole problem started with the constitutional changes in 1989. The main problem in Kosova bears the date of 23rd of March, 1989, when the constitution was changed. To return to your question, what you are presenting and the reality in Kosova, there is a discrepancy between the two. A population which had the Albanian language as the official one, the official language of teaching, becomes a language of a province. It was being dictated to the population as a second or third language, unimportant. On the basis of this principle, in 1991, the reality was different. The schools were divided into schools for the Serbs and schools for the Albanians; and this created a reality of division which was painful, which was brutal, because -- because the elementary school pupils were divided by a wall. There was no communication between them. The fact that it happened showed that the reality on paper and the reality on the ground were two completely different things. And you who have been away from Kosova in Belgrade, you did not -- you do not know the reality on the ground in Kosova. That is why we cannot talk about papers, the reality on paper. And the constitutional changes then. We can speak about a reality which was completely different from what was approved of in the constitution. But the key to all -- everything that followed is the changes in the constitution. It wasn't a semantical problem, but it was an issue of the brutally intervention -- brutal intervention in the life of the Kosovars. If I may say, the feeling among the population of Kosova after these changes, it was -- it was the feeling created among the population of the brutality of the police and the military, and that was also deduced from how they had behaved in Croatia and Bosnia. There was no need for brutality because the divisions that were created were a bit strange and unacceptable for a state, for a country, which wants to develop as one. The arrogance of the Serbian state was expressed on the kids, on schools, on the institutions. And the bottom line is that the difference between the reality on paper and the reality on the ground was huge. And if I could tell you that if anyone deserves credit for the independence of Kosova, it's not the Albanians who deserve it, it's the arrogance and the brutality of the Serbs. The independence was a product of the toughness and brutality of the Serbian regime. It was a product of the state which did not consider the Albanians as its own citizens. And the person who was sitting behind you, Mr. Djordjevic, should know better this situation because the independence of Kosova is also partly due to his behaviour because they considered the Albanians not as their own citizens, the authorities in Serbia, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I believe I have to surprise you by saying that I agree with a great deal of what you said, the only thing I would hold against you is mentioning my client, since as a lawyer, you know of the principle of presumption of innocence. Hence, Mr. Djordjevic is here to see whether he is guilty or not. Therefore, I will not develop that topic further.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Because I do not know Mr. Djordjevic or I never heard of him before, but simply because he was part of the state structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: There will be questions to that effect as well, but let's go back to the point concerning which I agree with you. The 1989 constitutional changes was the thing which in the minds of most intellectuals in Kosovo was what changed the situation on the grounds. Basically the situation was changed de facto and de jure. It wasn't different to what was in the constitution. It did do away with a certain degree of autonomy in Kosovo which had existed in the previous constitution often referred to the 1974 constitution, the communist one. We would agree that the Albanian population was not happy even with that constitution, but under that constitution, it enjoyed greater rights than under the 1989 constitution, which when implemented, provoked the reaction. That's why I said we agree on that. My next question has to do with the school curriculum which is something that you failed to mention. I don't remember any longer whether it was 1990 or 1991 but --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1991 or 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: -- when there was some discussion of the textbooks purchased in Albania proper in the bilingual schools. The Serb authorities had nothing to do with the way natural sciences or math was dealt with in those textbooks, these are objective sciences much as physics or biology. But when it comes to history and geography, one could come across certain maps showing greater Albania. Do you recall that? Do you recall the textbooks and the discussion which ensued indicating the existence of such maps that was carried by certain electronic media?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to interpret -- translate in my head in the different languages, let's speed things up. First of all, you know the declaration of the Albanian parties in 1990 and the principle of Kosovo republic within a federation or confederation. As for the textbooks, perhaps there may have been certain incidences or occurrences. But to take textbooks from Albania at that time would have been a crazy thing. It was no -- it was not necessary. In the 1990s, we had staff, we had people who could produce sound textbooks. The problem is not the curriculum, but the problem was in the population. What was it that the Republic of Serbia and Milosevic were trying to do? The fact is that they did not see the Albanians as their citizens. That was the core of the problem. The school curriculum and curricula in general were not at that core of that problem. The problem was that the state abolished certain freedoms in 1989 and 1990 and that was done by virtue of taxes. As Derida [phoen] would say, you never know when one ends up because you start with something and it keeps rolling. That was the main problem in the eyes of the citizens of Kosovo. You said that some people wanted more. Of course in Serbia there were people like that. In Croatia as well. There are always people who want more. But there was the political party agenda or platform which was in existence in 1990, and that platform was against confederation, or in the state destroyed the idea of a civic state. That is the nucleus of the problem that that political system had. I'm positive that that group -- that group is something that caused everything that followed resulting in the eventual independence of Kosova. That was basically the gist of the problem. It's not the education or the curricula, it's the civil rights that were at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm ready to accept that. What I believe is important to say at this point is that the Albanian political programs and, to use your own wording when you say some people wanted something or more, i.e., they wanted a republic of Kosovo or an independent Kosovo, that request has been with us as of 1980s?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: So what?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So nothing. I'm just saying it's been with us since the 1980s.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Does one have to wage a war over that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that that request was in place as of the 1980s. My question concerning that is: Did any representatives or the Albanian population in general - in the course of their demonstrations in the 1980s or say, 1997, in the course of the student demonstrations or civil demonstrations, any demonstrations for that matter in Kosovo - did they ever want to go below the bench-mark they set? And you mentioned on that afternoon when you sat down with the representatives of the security service, the request being a republic of Kosovo or an independent Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Believe me, that was back in 1989 and 1990, none of the Albanian parties - and I mean those who knew what powers the Republic of Serbia or the army of the Republic of Yugoslavia had - did not go for the maximum. It was clear what it would mean to have independent Kosova. Independent Kosova would mean splitting Kosova down the middle losing everything that you had previously created. Therefore, we knew what had the maximum claims might be. Nevertheless, there were people in Belgrade who thought differently and this is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question, your principle statement in 2001 -- that's the one I'm talking about when your friend Abrahams, your acquaintance, came to see you as well as Mr. Jonathan Sutch. Did he express any misgivings concerning the policy pursued by the DSK party headed from the Serbian viewpoints at the time by Mr. Ibrahim Rugova, he was the party president, wasn't he. As far as I know, you said that his political goals were to achieve everything by peaceful means without a war, almost Gandhi-like. And that was his method of achieving the political goals of the Albanian people. I don't agree with that, but I'd still like to know what exactly you wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Let's put it this way, after Dayton, Serbia displayed such a degree of arrogance towards Kosovo and the Albanians in Kosova that they failed to mention Kosova as a problem at all, they ignored the whole situation as much as they could. And that is why Rugova was entirely powerless following Dayton. In Serbia, they weren't willing to have a peaceful process to try and achieve peace. They all believed they were fully in control over the Albanians, they were controlling all the businesses and everything. One thing they forgot was people needed jobs, people needed employment. In 1997, when the first generation of university students graduated in the parallel system, Serbia refused to recognise their diplomas, so what were those people supposed to do? Go abroad or wage war; there was no other choice. Life was far too dynamic for those young people to be able to afford to stand there and then listen to someone from Belgrade. The police, the Serbian services in Kosovo, were entirely corrupted. Those who were sitting there in some virtual way held sway over Kosovo, but the reality on the ground was brutal. That is why the president, Ibrahim Rugova, after Dayton was politically dead. It was only a matter of time when something would start happening. Why had nothing happened up to Dayton? Everything had been fully under control. The expectations were that Serbia would come to its wits, after Bosnia and after Croatia in a political sense and that an opening would be found for peace. Stanisic himself said it. I don't have the power, someone else has the power to restore peace. Milosevic is the man, with his wife and another person whose name I can't remember. Hence, in 1997 we knew where the red line was. There was no way anyone could try and artificially affect the situation in Kosovo any more. In 1996 there was the intermediation effort, meaning San Egidio, they wanted to sign an agreement for people to go back to their buildings, the schools. But they didn't. They opened a single institute yet all of the other buildings remained closed.
