What you say -- what there was on paper and the actual brutal reality the brutality on the ground were two different things. And that's why the war came about. And that's why what happened after 1997 eventually materialised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Speaking of persons who had a role to play, you mentioned Milosevic, you mentioned the late president of Kosovo, Rugova. I would like to make a reference here to probably the richest Albanian Mr. Bakalli do you not believe that he too was a man who indirectly, through the Russians, joined forces with the Serbs against Albanian interests? Can you please briefly explain.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Pacolli came from Moscow via Milosevic to make an offer, and he offered something that was not feasible. He was offering the same thing that Serbia had actually abolished back in 1989. This wasn't a realistic thing. Bakalli himself met Milosevic in February 1998 in his own home, as a matter of fact, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to Bakalli; that is what I'm trying to get you to tell me about. What he was offering was a return to the level of autonomy prior to 1998 and 1999, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No. Listen, as far as the political project was concerned, it was about details. He was offering something that was unacceptable. In 1998 it was too late. There were people there. The KLA were already in the woods. There were over 25.000 persons who were armed. It was too late for an effort like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Indeed. Nevertheless, it wasn't the KLA that were in charge of everything. The KLA and its political leaders, not the military leaders, were not involved in that.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: It was impossible, no one really accepted them as leaders. The first contacts came as late as May 1998. It was too late. It was too late for any agreements. We were tabling an offer for a peace project. We -- they even wanted today second some of our even people, six of them as a matter of fact, we offered intermediaries. We had it all out on the table and they threw it all away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going into that. I know what Serbia's position was at the time, and you are entirely right. The mediators were unacceptable in view of Serbia's policy at the time. Those were diplomats who Serbia saw as being in the service of the Kosovar and Albanian interest alone. So that was the reason for their refusal.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: It wasn't about Albanian interest, it was about violations of human rights. What does that have to do with Albanian interests?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Call it what you like, I know they weren't acceptable candidates. I'm trying not to waste any time, and I'm trying to avoid you having to stay here tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question. Mr. Bujar Bukoshi, he was frequently in touch with you and you often went to see him in Germany, Switzerland, something like that?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, a total of three meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Who is Bujar Bukosi and why Bujar Bukosi?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: What do you mean "why"?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: With you.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Oh why, with me. Oh yes. At the time, he was Kosovar's prime minister in exile. As far as an illegal points of concern, you should ask him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: One speaker at a time, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You say you were arrested today, but you say --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: One speaker at a time, please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic and Mr. Haxhiu, we are translating into a number of languages and you are speaking together in direct conversation and not allowing time for the process to catch up to you. Therefore, we are not getting down on the transcript all that should be. If you could each try to pause before you come in --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I have a suggestion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You should take your ear phone and listen in English and when it stop, we can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That might work, yes, but I think both of you need to be aware of the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we continue in B/C/S then? Bujar Bukoshi. You invited him after, as you said, several interviews; you were called for interviews, they would hold you for two hours, then you would go away. You said [indiscernible] today, I don't think there was any ill intent on your part, maybe it was just the way it felt for you at the time. Why did you call Bujar Bukoshi and not, for example, Kosovar's president Mr. Rugova or both?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: If you read my statement properly, I sent the letter to Mr. Rugova but not to Mr. Bukoshi because it was dangerous, risky, to send letters; therefore, I contacted him personally in Switzerland. In the letter, I explained in detail the problem to Mr. Rugova. But I felt more confident, I mean, I had great ties with Mr. Bukoshi and Mr. Agani because of past relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Why were you the choice of the Serb security forces? Why not president Rugova or Mr. Bukoshi for that matter? Why did they choose you? What did you mean to them at the time? What was the reason that the leadership of the security service or the security agency, BIA - that was what they were called at the time - contacted you as opposed to any officials, if obviously they were after negotiations? What was it that they knew about you that made you a good choice in their eyes, a good source of information, and why did they ask to meet you?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: They didn't choose me; but when I was arrested, it was me who said the time has come for us to engage in a dialogue, and that the way you have chosen would lead us to war. They said, Who can build this dialogue? And I mentioned some names. And they said, Can we have a meeting so that we start this thing? I said, Yes, but we are rather late, I said. I'm an open-minded person, I don't have -- I don't suffer from the idea of Balkan conspiracy. Therefore it was a very straightforward dialogue. When I was arrested, I said, Today you maltreated me, but I think this course will lead to war and that it is high time we engage in dialogue to discuss concrete political issues. Because even as it is, we are rather late. It was not they who chose me, but it was me who came up with this idea curing my arrest. And they asked me, Can you do this? And I proposed Bakalli and Mr. Agani; it is as simple as that. And so two meetings took place, and that was it. I didn't contact them again, neither did they contact me again. The situation was a dramatic one, a settlement had to be found, when the Serbs saw that they erred with the students, when they maltreated them, the situation developed in a dramatic way. So they were after a rapid solution. They saw that they no longer controlled the situation so there is no conspiracy at stake at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I had in mind. What I meant was any political status that you may have enjoyed at the time, any relations that you may have and obtained with certain persons. Perhaps something that I haven't brought up so far. That's what I was asking about. But now you've explained that. My next question. The first meeting that came about, you said Mr. Gajic was there, Mr. Hadjic too, you were there, Mr. Bakalli. Are you certain, personally, about the identities of those persons that their names were Hadjic, Gajic, that they held the positions that they said they held? Were you certain about their identities under those people were legal and authorised representatives of that service or agency? Did you perhaps ask any additional questions later on in order to find out who it was that you had been talking to?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I thought that they were who they were because Zoran Stijovic was also present at the meeting. And I saw Mr. Gajic in a photo later or newspapers when he gave interviews on the situation of Kosova. But I never saw Mr. Hadjic again after that. Therefore, I cannot say whether that was his true identity. But that was how he introduced himself, and I took note of his name in my notebook. Because I wanted to be accurate in what was going on. I didn't want any misinterpretation. I took down everything single word they said. They didn't take any notes. I may suppose as Mr. Bakalli said later, maybe they had microphones and maybe they recorded everything, but I personally wrote down every single word that was said at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Up until the moment you were interviewed and then you said "its high time we engage in a dialogue," in negotiations, and some time elapsed before the meeting occurred, quite some time in fact. At that point in time, did you get in touch with anyone or try to get anyone organised, apart from Bakalli, in order to agree what the platform, what the position would be should it ever come to a meeting like that? Or was it more of an improvised thing going on that night?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: The proposal I made during my arrest, I never thought it would be taken seriously, to be frank with you. And I didn't think they would summon us, but they called us after a long time when the -- probably when the situation grew very exacerbated and they wanted to find a way out of it. We didn't have any contacts, I didn't receive any calls from them, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We'll be going back to that at a later stage. Which dates do you see as the date the KLA came into existence?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Do you want it in the context of historical development or the patriotic context? Because we had to do with different realities. A wishful reality and the factual reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I want to know about the KLA.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: In real terms, the KLA came into existence after the events of the 1st of October. And the brutal approach used against the students. 1st of October, 1997. Everything that happened before consisted of individual efforts, but the armed resistance which was related to the KLA because due to absence of any other solutions came after the intervention, brutal intervention, by the police of the 1st of October. But it became more massive after the killing of the Jashari family in March 1992 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 1998. Correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- when everybody wanted to take up arms because they could take it no longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Nevertheless, if we look at these statements, we find you saying this: You were aware of the entire negative aspect of the story involving the establishment of KLA and their actives in the area. And you even went as far as to say that you deliberately misinterpreted some bits at some meetings in Malisevo, perhaps they talked about the idea of a greater Albania and you left that out because you knew that that would cause a lot of negative commotion among the international players. I understand your position, you're a Kosovar Albanian and a patriot. Nevertheless, what I would like you to share with us is this. I'm not talking about your perspective, I'm talking about you in your capacity as a journalist. What was this negative context in which the KLA was involved among the international players present there at the beginning? Could you please comments on that.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: They were entirely unknown, nobody knew who they were. At the beginning, we really thought they were ex-military from the Yugoslav Army. But when we realised that they were young people, young boys who had just graduated from the parallel universities, we realised that the situation was out of control, that it was a matter of venting out their pent-up hatred against what the Serbs had done to them in the last years. And all these young people, when I saw them, personally saw them, I was really taken aback at what I saw. That's why when I interpreted, I tried to be rational and not be effected by the irrationality of the time. Imagine if I interpreted to the international representatives the concept of the greater Albania. How to explain it to someone from the KLA. At that time, I wrote an article, a very strong article, against such an idea which I considered dangerous. For us, it was a matter of survival, and not of grand political projects that for the moment were more than an illusion. I'm telling you that there were people who "helped" us, assisted us, with their arrogance; and what is described, if I might say, dishonest policy which originated in Belgrade. The best way to put it would be: Look, people, they know not what they do. And I think that they didn't know what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You were a journalist with the Bota e Re; right?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: In 1988 I started my internship in Bota e Re newspaper, a student newspaper. That is where I started to learn journalism.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What about 1997 and 1998, working as editor in Koha e Ditore?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: In 1997 we founded the Koha Ditore newspaper. At that time it was called Koha Javore, weekly time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that in your capacity at editor you're monitoring all the electronic and the printed media in Kosovo at the time including Bota e Re.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: At the time, Bota e Re didn't exist as a newspaper. It was closed down in 1990 by Rrahman Morina and the former regime. Also the front cover page which showed three overturned chairs when we asked the resignation of these three persons. Kole Shiroka, Rrahman Morina --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the third, I didn't get the name. The interpreter did not understand the name of the third person you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ali Shukrije.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Adrian Krasniqi, does that name ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I knew his name because I published it in my newspaper, it is said that he organised an action somewhere in the vicinity of Decan, but I never met him in person, and I don't know who he is. I only know that as the people say now, he was one of the first members of the armed group. If I recall right, his action was organised in 1993 or 1994. I couldn't be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that his photograph was published in a magazine wearing a military uniform with KLA insignia? It couldn't possibly have been in 1993, there was no KLA around in 1993. The magazine published his photograph carrying a hand-held rocket launcher, automatic weapons. And the caption underneath that photo read "Adrian in action" do you remember that? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Do you want to talk about wishful Balkan wishes or facts? In fact, there are individuals who in reality --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Facts here.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I don't think he was a member of the KLA. There were many individuals in exile who had similar wishes, and they bought uniforms for 100 francs, but there was no military formation as such. In Germany and Switzerland for example, they managed to -- they managed to form a wishful military formation, but there was no active military formation. The military elements were imbued in members -- former members of the police or the army, but they were imprisoned, and in the period after 1992 that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that this man Adrian Krasniqi was killed in 1997? Are you aware of the fact that the electronic media in the Albanian language, in the printed media, he was made out to be a victim of the Serbian policy and a young student who was killed amid student rallies? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I said that his picture was published in a newspaper Zeri i Kosoves in Switzerland. And it wasn't published in the newspapers in Kosovo. But as regards the action that he undertook, that was published in our newspaper, but we published the official version. That according to the police he had attacked a police station. So let's not talk about imaginary military formations. I'd like to say that the real KLA is a product of after the 1st of October. As it to what people wrote on paper in Switzerland or Germany, that's another issue. Completely different matter. If we start exploring that avenue, then we may think that -- we may come to a conclusion that the KLA was formed even before 1989. But the real facts are a different thing. The KLA is a product of the Serb repression and of these people, it's a product of the post-Dayton peaceful policies of Ibrahim Rugova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As a journalist, did you know that KLA members carried out kidnappings of Albanian civilians and civilians of other ethnic groups? Do you know of the existence of any detention camps? And did you know that throughout the period they kept attacking Serbian police and military forces in the guerilla type actions? They blocked roads, set up check-points?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, they did that after 1998. After the Jashari family was attacked, people came out into the streets. They set up check-points, and it was a state of war. That's accurate. And we are speaking about the period after the first attack on the Jasharis, in January. And that was especially so when people came out onto the roads in the Drenica region. That's KLA members that is. And I'm saying it again that this was the consequence of the Serb brutality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The 18th of June, 1998, the road between Pristina and Pec, you say that in the summer of 1998 you used that road to get to Malisevo, and that in Drenica and Orahovac, you saw the destruction caused by the Serb forces. Did you know that on that date, on that road, a civilian and police convoy was attacked in Iglarevo? Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: On the 16th, no. There were incidents after the 1998, after May 1998. I do not recall any names, but there was fighting. There was fighting, yes. And sporadic attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that the KLA blocked the road between Pristina and Pec at Lapusnik when going from the direction of Pristina and at Dolac when one goes from Pec? They set up barricades of stones, tree trunks, car tires, and mined them. You apparently used some of those roads wherein travelling with the diplomat, as you said yourself.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, after the road was blocked, then the famous sentence came into being that the peace and war in Kosovo is named Lapusnik. If you remember, Mr. Holbrooke said that. Then you may know that the notorious offensive of the Serb forces took place after which -- following which there were so many killings. There I saw terrifying things. I went around those mountains with David Slinn, a diplomat, and I could not believe where brutality could go at what stage, at what level it could go. I never thought what I saw. Whole villages, following the June offensive, were burned to the ground. There was not a single house which was not unburned. In the Rahovec region, in Malishevo region, in the Komorane/Prishtina region, all houses were burned to the ground, and I saw it with my own eyes. On the way to -- that was to go on the way to persuading the KLA to set up a team to negotiate a way out of this conflict. And we went to a village in the Malishevo region and we when to Drenica to talk to the other part of the KLA, Veton Surroi went there and Chris Hill went there. It was a catastrophe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We know that, and that is not in dispute. We found that in your statement. Am I right in saying that in June 1998 the traffic between Pristina and Prizren was made impossible, it was interrupted by the KLA and one had to go the round about way to get to Pristina from Prizren, in June 1998?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I received no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I just wanted to have that for the transcript. Am I right in saying that the village of Kijevo was blocked for a month?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's where the battle of Lapusnik took place. They are very close. And from there, the road was blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: While there were blocks on the road between Pec and Pristina, one could move between the two places only via Roxhaje and Kulla; am I correct? And I have in mind that Serbs could not use it.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: You could go by Brezovica, you could go via Prizren-Gjakove road, and also via Istoq. There were ways outs. Buy, in fact, the Serbs of Peje did not need to go to Prishtina because the situation was very grave. The Serbs did not move along the main road at the time. Serbs of Kijevo either went to Peje or they followed the Prizren-Gjakove road to go to Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Lapusnik, did you know that there was a KLA prison in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No, I've never visited a KLA prison there. I never thought that there could be prisons. I learned that when the accusations started against the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that many corpses of non-Albanians as well as Albanians were discovered in Lapusnik? Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I remember a press conference of the then-Prosecutor who was a Serb. She was so untrustful. I've never trusted her. I'm saying that if there was a shred of truth, she was the person who made the whole thing unbelievable. She had no credibility. She was the worst personality of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean Ms. Danica Maksimovic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that in July 1998, the KLA attacked and occupied Orahovac, Velika Hoca, Zociste [phoen], and Retimlje?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I was there personally with journalists of the BBC. No, it's not correct. I visited that place and there were 250 metres distance between the check-points. KLA and Serb forces. This was a day before the offensive when we visited the place. I visited Rahovec a day before the offensive. And there was no indication as to who was attacking. In my book I described in general the fighting in Rahovec, and I -- the strategy was that through Rahovec they could attack Malishevo and go towards Drenica, and the attack was planned because it was carried out within 24 hours. Because the tanks, a day before the interpretation that the KLA attacked Rahovec, the tanks left Prishtina and surrounded all the area in Malishevo from the other side. And the action was planned. For us who lived in Prishtina and who had access to information, and Mr. Agani I remember called me to his office, and he was informed by a captain of the army a day before the attacks started, and he had been told that the attack would start to destroy Rahovec. But this happened after the meeting between Bakalli, Surroi, Agani, in the Milosevic office, and then it finished in the white house. It wasn't that the KLA was attacked, but every single house was attacked and burned. It was civilian families who were killed. And there was a counter-effect of the whole thing that they had planned. And it's not true that -- there was fighting in Rahovec, but the attack was well planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Briefly then, your answer is no?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm positive about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You are positive in the "no," or are you positive about the things that you were saying?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Positive that the planning of such a large-scale military action was an earlier one. And I think that the signal was sounded by the international community in order to weaken the role of the KLA. And in real terms it was Mr. Holbrooke who did that. You may not recall the meeting of the 26th of May in the office of Milosevic of the group of Kosova in 1998 and then Mr. Clinton state secretary in Washington.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Malisevo, did you know that there was a KLA prison in Malisevo?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: If you lived in the circumstances I lived, you don't have believed that, because in fact Kosova itself was a large prison. There were 2 million people who were imprisoned in that prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: For Albanians? What prison in Kosovo? I'm asking about Malisevo.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: The whole of Kosova was a prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But do you know where a small prison in Malisevo were Serbs from Orahovac were kept? It was small and run by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No, there are many reasons why I don't know. It was a minor event in the context of a horrible situation. That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the KLA in 1998 kidnapped a full busload of workers and miners from the mines of Belacevac, and they were all subsequently killed, they also worked at the --

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: The KLA people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: -- of Obilic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witnesses are overlapping yet again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They entered this thermo-electron plant, but as you are putting to me, they kidnapped a busload of workers and miners, this is not true. They entered there, I don't know if there were any casualties, because it was daily phenomenon to hear of killings and murders, so it didn't make news, so to say. It was -- it happened in 1998, this, it was something that happens in every war. People are killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I was asking you. Concerning the methods of waging the war by the KLA, first of all, was it a guerilla type of warfare? And second of all, that KLA members took to the forests often with civilians changing their military uniforms for civilian clothes as Mr. Zyrapi described in one of his testimonies?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I wasn't present in any such situation when they may have changed their uniforms. But that they waged a guerilla warfare, that's true. They were not a military -- regular military formation, but the Serb army was so strong that it was hardly likely for any KLA groups to face up to them. But the worse of all this was that the Serb military and army and police didn't fight with the KLA, but with the civilians, and their brutality was directed against the civilians. That's why the war -- they lost the war. They won the war against the KLA, but they lost their battle of the war against the human being. The problem is that they didn't reckon with the people of the population of the 21st century. We have two different philosophical notions. They won the war against the KLA, but they lost it to the people of Kosova. That's why they are here at The Hague Tribunal. That's why we have the independence of Kosova now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It is almost time for our break, just before that, I have one more question. Let's go back to the afternoon when you were in the house together with the representatives of the Serb security forces and Mr. Bakalli. You and Bakalli were the only Albanians who talked to them on that occasion. What legitimacy did you hold, you and Mr. Bakalli have in order to appear as the representatives of the Albanian population? Did you have any, as a matter of fact?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: The time context or frame is something else. I want to explain to you that every public person in Kosova had a kind of role to play. I was the editor in chief of a newspaper, Mr. Bakalli was a public figure. Each of us tried to fight -- to find a peaceful way to the situation. I think that Mr. Rugova, Mr. Agani, and other gentlemen had their own channels of communication; but none of us had the courage to talk with the Serbs face to face. They did this either through mediations which sometimes create confusion and unclarity because they want to -- by all means to have positive results for themselves or for the others. But my experience is that direct contact is the best way to start negotiations for peace, but I think Serbia was not ready. We proposed six persons to them to start these negotiations, but we never received any feedback from them as to why these negotiations never became a reality. We proposed Mr. Ibrahim Rugova, Bakalli, Fehmi Agani, Veton Surroi, Bujar Bukoshi, and a second one whose name I don't remember; they asked who -- which of the Serbs can be of the negotiation table? We said to them, It's not us that will decide which of you will be there. They didn't agree that Bob Norman and Nick Hill be the intermediators in these talks. They considered Bob Norman as a US diplomat being an anti-Serb one. I don't know for what reason. It was not a question of legitimacy, it was a question of taking an initiative when one hopes to find a peaceful solution, he tries. Now, this question may have a meaning, but not your question. But not -- your question. But not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Just before the break, you and Mr. Bakalli put forth the maximum of the requests of the Albanian community in Kosovo, had those people there told you, Yes we would accept that and let's start with the negotiations as of tomorrow and we will create a confederation, would you have been able to accept such a proposal? I agree that these people representing the Serb side were Serb representatives, mediators of sorts, but what if they had the authority, the power, to approve your request and say, As of tomorrow we start the negotiation process. What would you have said?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: We knew what the situation was like on the ground. We knew what the real possibilities were for us. We knew the stand of the international community. There was no one among the internationals that ever mentioned the independence of Kosova. We knew that the process couldn't be complete without the participation of the international community. The fact that we made a proposal and proposed some names who would be involved in these negotiations, six names actually, that was where our work ended. That was our initiative. You may not understand what this -- how seriously we were taken by the Serbs, how scornfully we were looked upon by them. They felt very powerful vis-a-vis a small and unarmed population. The main problem in this generation of politicians was total disrespect for the human being. They never regarded the human being as a real being. That was, in my opinion, the problem with this generation of politicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will continue after the break hoping that we would be able to conclude your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. We will have our second break now. The Chamber would point out that we've been silent, allowing each of you full rein. Now, we hope that that will bear the fruit of a conclusion today. We adjourn now and resume at 5 minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The witness and I have just entered a very comprehensive debate. Please interrupt me if you think I'm going too far, getting carried away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will try to wrap up this set of questions about the attempted negotiations, about Brezovica, let's move on to that. It was only you and Mr. Bakalli that went to Brezovica. Why didn't none of the other prominent Kosovar Albanian leaders join you given the fact that the meeting was attended by Jovica Stanisic as well? There had been request by the Serb side perhaps or something else, could you enlighten us on that, sir?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: In fact, that request was presented to Mr. Bakalli. They said they wanted to continue what we started but with Mr. Stanisic; and when Mr. Stanisic arrived that day, he offered us a meeting with Mr. Milosevic, but we refused that. It appeared -- it would appear that he did not have a mandate to negotiate. He had a limited mandate. Although, I believe that I saw him for the first time when he was sent to Bosnia during an assembly in Bosnia, and I heard his name in 1995 during a Serb conference. He had gone to mediate there, and it had stuck on my mind, the name, and I considered him as an important person. But later on, I didn't hear any more about him. I didn't know much about him. But during his political interpretation, it was correct, he had a rationale behind what he was saying; but he was limited in what he wanted to achieve, and the outcome was rather bad, very grave, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Another brief question, very brief. The focus of the talk was between Mr. Bakalli and Mr. Stanisic; right?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: During the first half of the meeting, he wanted to have a tête-à-tête with Mr. Bakalli. It appeared that he wanted to reassure himself in that meeting, he didn't find that during that part of the meeting, so he then came together with Mr. Bakalli to a joint meeting. I heard from Mr. Bakalli what they discussed during the first half of meeting, and obviously he had told him the same thing that we had proposed during the first meeting in his flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that in your statement later on, we know that. We know that. Can you please just clarify another sentence that I came across in your statement. When you were driving back to Pristina, Bakalli and you, you were shaking with fear. That is precisely what you said. What sort of fear? Had any threats been made? What was all that about?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: In fact, in Bakalli's flat, Mr. Hadjic pointed his finger at me and said, If anyone knows about this meeting - and he was pointing his finger at me - you won't be the same person that you are. This was not reminded to me again, but the atmosphere of the place where the meeting took place was not nice. So he used the metaphor of going to war rather badly. And that influenced the atmosphere of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Clear enough. Clear enough. My next question, it's about the fact that you were sentenced and there was a fine to pay, you never paid the fine, but I want to ask you about something else. You said the trial took place in 22nd March, 1992. You know, we lawyers try to work according to rules. On the calendar it was a Monday, but let's not make any mistakes about that, it may have been a Sunday. Was that perhaps the 21st of March, 1999, when you were standing before a judge? And not the 22nd as the statement reflects. That's what my question is about. So it was a Sunday, that much is certain; right? Because your statement says it was the 22nd of March.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: It was the 21st, the 21st as I said a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's fine, that's fine then. All right. Let's move on to my next question. Your statement says 200.000 German marks. That was his punishment and yours was 25.000 German marks. Could we agree that you were wrong? You said about 300.000 German marks. It was a lot. I'm telling you it was more, it was 420.000 for the magazine and for you personally it was 110.000. Can we agree on that? And for the magazine it would have amounted to 26.000 dollars and 7.200 dollars for you. Those were the figures reported in the foreign press about the dollars, and this was all pursuant to Article 67 of the Law on Information, the famous law apparently designed or devised by Minister Vujacic who was then a member of the Serb radical party. Can we first of all agree on these basic facts just in order to have some degree objectivity here? 420.000 for the magazine and --

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: If you remember, at the time there was a huge inflation with regard to the dinar, and the amount, the amount that was assigned one day, the value fell by 50 per cent the following day. But the law you were referring to was not implemented towards me, but also it was implemented in the case of Blic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That was my next question as a matter of fact. It wasn't just about Blic, there was the Kikinda paper, Pancevac, many from Novi Sad, many newspapers in electronic media that were blamed on the same law?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: This was a series of sentences during that month.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: There's another detail in relation to this. That's right, and we 're about to wrap up. It wasn't just against Albanian media, but also Serb media. The daily telegraph from Serbia was also fined. All right. I'm moving on to my next topic. Can we agree that you were made to answer under the provisions of the misdemeanours law because that's what it. It was a misdemeanours court; it wasn't a textbook court of law?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: The law was a catastrophe. According to the law, they found an excuse. The law was voted in the most brutal way in Serbia. It was a fast-track procedure, and the law was passed within a week and the --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I know. Thank you, thank you. Thank you for that. Let us just try to agree on this: The charge you were facing causing interethnic hatred, under that law, they took into account the magazine that published your piece entitled, I think, "Kosovo Awaiting a Dispatch from NATO," something along these lines. But other thing that was typical, I want to know if you remember that, you had to put up a defence within 24 hours of the misdemeanours, proceedings request? I don't know if you remember that. It literally had to be done within 24 hours, you had to mount a defence within 24 hours? If you don't remember, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: No, no, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It's fine.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Friday we published the article on the second page of the newspaper. On Saturday the fast-track procedure was sent to us that I had to report to court and that was -- I had to report to court urgently on Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It was a Sunday; right? That's right. And it was the duty misdemeanours judge who was there, this was perfectly normal institution at the time - I have to tell you, in case you don't remember, because I see that you were slightly surprised by the fact - that the trial -- the hearing took place on the Sunday. But this was a duty judge. That's right. Thank you very much. I'm not asking you any further questions about this. We need to leave some time for my learned friend Mr. Neuner to ask additional questions on his part should he have any prompted by my own cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have Exhibit D003-3235 pulled up on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What is this about? This is an additional statement or an addendum to a statement made in the November 2006 by Mr. Haxhiu to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go to page 2. The next one, please. Thank you. Could we please have the Albanian too, if available. If not, I understand the witness speaks very good English. No Albanian. All right. I will just press on in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at what you said there, this is in the supplement, the 24th of March period to the 2nd of April. Let's try to translate that. From the 24th of March to 2nd of April 1999 you were in the basement so you did not see what was going on in Pristina. When you left Pristina on the 2nd of April, 1999, he saw older fat men in green uniforms wearing masks and so on and so forth. This is not the point because you keep talking about that in your earlier statements and the evidence you gave, you realised at one point there was most probably paramilitaries. But there's something else I'd like to ask you about where you said about the 24th of March to 2nd of April they really had no knowledge of what was going on in Pristina. Today you spoke a great deal about precisely this period, including the murder of one of your guards on the premises of your publishing house. And then you talked about the fact that you went from your house to that writer's house. And why is it phrased this way in the statement, since today you told us something else altogether? Can you tell us about that? What does this mean?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: What is it you're unclear about? Which part?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: One thing that I'm unclear about: You were telling us today that you were walking around Pristina, you even went to the newspaper headquarters. At the time, your guard was killed, body-guard was killed. It says here that in the period between 24th of March and the 2nd of April, you were hiding in the became therefore you were not able to see what was going on in Pristina until you left the basement on the 2nd of April, and we know that you left for Macedonia. I'm asking you this: Do you see that the discrepancy there? That's all I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: There's into discrepancy. Look at the dates. On the 24th when the bombing started, let me clarify. I thought that when bombing was start there will be freedom of movement, so I had left to meet my journalists at the Koha Ditore offices. And at 9.30 on the 25th, I had planned to get out and go to the offices of the newspaper. On the 25th, I went from where I stayed the night to the Dardanija neighbourhood. Then I stayed two other days and the following day I went to Kodra e Diellit. I never said that I went out in town because it was not possible. On the 25th in the evening, 9.30 p.m., at about 9.00 p.m., some young men broke into shops and businesses, and we could see from the windows of where we were staying because all the lights were off, and we could see -- we could see what was going on in the street. And I said that we could see that the businesses were being broken into and looted and so on. But I never said for a moment that I went out in town to take a walk. If you consider it a walk or an outing from when I left from one flat to another, then that's what it is. But a walk has a different meaning, or going out to town has got another meaning, and what the situation was another.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, I misworded my previous statement. What I had in mind was you moving about town because the paragraph suggests that you spent all this time in a single room in this flat. Therefore, you did not know at the time what was going on in Pristina. And that is the difference that I'm trying to highlight. You spoke a lot about Julian Braithwaite [indiscernible]. Ambassador Wolfgang Petritsch, he was the Ambassador at the time, we don't have that much time, and I would not like to ask any further questions about this because it was dealt with in the addendum, I would like to appeal to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Briefly I would like to ask the Chamber just in order to make sure I don't take up the next 15 or 20 minutes, to have this addendum admitted into evidence because of the substance of the addendum and what the witness said about it. D003-3235. He speaks about Abe Satotsi [as interpreted] Julian Braithwaite --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat the names that he just mentioned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you repeat those names, please, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I repeat, could you please repeat the names that you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour. The university [indiscernible] is mentioned here in this addendum; the Pale university; Julian Braithwaite; David Slinn; Jonathan Weiss; Jan Kickert, a witness who appeared here; Albert Rohan; and Ambassador Wolfgang Petritsch. I could cut the time short and not ask the questions that will clarify this. I won't be asking those questions, but I would like to have this addendum exhibited instead, the date is the 7th of November, 1996. It was 2006. It was given by this witness, and may that please be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D227, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I just wanted to say to ease the burden for my learned colleague. At this point in time, the Prosecution has probably one question only, so you are please going on as much as you wish to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you, my learned friend. As the addendum has just been admitted, we are probably gaining at least 20 minutes. I will have another brief question to ask most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you have any information indicating how many Serbs left Kosovo after the Kumanovo Agreement, Serbs and other non-Albanians?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all the other microphones be switched off, please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot be firm about the number, but I know that there was such movement, especially in Central Kosova and Northern Kosova, so please don't ask me about the exact figure because I don't have it. I know that there was a movement immediately following the Kumanovo Agreement, especially after the 14th or the 15th. There was movement on tractors from Northern Kosova in the direction of Serbia; however, part of them, the Serbs, even before that during the Milosevic regime had already bought some houses in Serbia. So for some it was surprising that they were leaving, but for some it was clear that they were fleeing because of corruption, fear of prosecution, and so on, and because of guilt.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My last question for you today: You still work as a journalist I assume, don't you? Do you have any information on the number of Serbs and other non-Albanians who returned to Kosovo after this?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Not many. Kosova is not a pleasant place to live in, even for Albanians themselves, let alone the Serbs. It is a very poor country facing serious problems for all of its inhabitants. In my opinion, the Balkans is still a primitive concept of living. People do not have many options and opportunities in the Balkans. What would my suggestion to the Serbs be in real terms. My answer would be, Kosova has no meaning without the Serbs. However, it is very difficult to live in a poor country with little prospective, especially for the young people. In my opinion, people who have lived in Kosova with Serbs know of the charm of cohabitation, but this charm is lost due to this economic, political, and so on problems. So Serbia would be the prospective for the young people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiu, thank you for your evidence. I wish I could say that many of the things that you talked about today were possible and that there might be better times ahead; nevertheless, if we want to start seeking answers to a lot of other questions, that would merely prolong our debate which would then take days. We have heard from you today everything that has any relevance to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, I complete my cross-examination of this witness, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Djordjevic. Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Just briefly, Mr. Haxhiu, you were asked by my learned colleague just a moment ago about your period while you were hiding in houses or various houses or basements in Pristina. Could you just explain again, what was the reason for you going a little bit undercover, if I may call it?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: The first reason would be that we were exposed as workers in the newspaper. Second reason would be the fact that my lawyer was killed. And the third reason was the war itself. Another reason would be the advice that we received from our international friends. I was amongst those who was at risk. I always led a public, open life. Whatever my views were, I published them in my newspaper. And on the 22nd, I published on the front page of a newspaper "NATO Air: Just Do It." So a friend of mine advised me, said, Listen, this is not a good message that you are sending to the people of the Milosevic regime, so I would suggest that you better go into hiding and look after your life. So these would be the reasons, minus the main one, that of the war situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. I tried to understand this answer. You say you were exposed as workers of the newspaper. Exposed to whom?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Koha Ditore always had a clear-cut stance against the Milosevic regime and the brutal acts of the authorities for years. Therefore, this course of criticism, in a sense that we never went out of the boundaries of the lawful, instead we discussed in our newspaper cases of violation of human rights, police brutality against civilians, and so on; and we promoted the idea of respecting human rights, Albanians, and whatever -- whoever lived in Kosova. So in this way, we were exposed to the views of the authorities. I was the one who designed the policy in the editorial office, and that's why in a way, I take the blame on myself for this. Those who made public their views against the Milosevic regime existed even in Belgrade. An editor in chief there was also killed. So fear comes first, braveness comes second. So that's why I was forced to move from one house to another in order to convince myself psychologically that they may not find me. Because in a way, we were all killed. They could kill us whenever they wanted, but this fear, fleeing from one apartment to another, in a way created a sense of security in the people. So as I said, fear was the one that was dominating at the time. Not only with me, but with everybody in Kosova at the time. There were a few political figures, public figures in Kosova, that openly expressed their views against the Milosevic regime. I'm not speaking about the Serbian people, about the Serbian civilians, but about the regime, the Milosevic regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Is it correct that at some point in time, your -- the fact that you are still living was disputed?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I later learned, now maybe this is not the place to say, but I realised later that I was amongst names of those in a list of people who were wanted dead. My name was also on this list. I don't want to deal with this part because I don't think it's relevant for the Trial Chamber and for this specific case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Then I maybe misunderstood you. I thought you had told me this morning, before we met briefly before you went to court, that at some point in time at the beginning of the war after the 24th of March, 1999, somebody had made an announcement that you were dead?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Yes. On the 29th of March at 3.30 I was announced dead by Jamie Shea and Welby [phoen] at a NATO press conference held in Brussels. The statement said the following: Yesterday four intellectuals, Kosovan intellectuals were killed, Fehmi Agani, Baton Haxhiu, and two others. This happened after the funeral of Bajram Kelmendi, a well-known lawyer and humanist from Kosovo. So the so-called death, my death situation, went on until the 2nd of April when I crossed into Macedonia. If you asked me what death means, I can tell you that I know that there is spiritual death and physical death. I personally was spiritually dead. A civilian like me and like others was spiritually dead. The way we lived in those difficult conditions, we had this feeling of being dead, not alive. We didn't have the opportunity to inform families that we were still alive or that we were well. People would go to my parents, to my family for condolences, to express their condolences for my death. So this is what war brings, things that should better be forgotten. So at this time I realise that there are two types of death, spiritual and physical death. In our case, we were alive, figuratively speaking, but that's when I realised that spirit is part of every human body that keeps you alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The declaration from NATO was issued in which year, please? You said 29th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Obviously the declaration was wrong in relation to the death of your person, but what about the other man you mentioned, Fehmi Agani and two others?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: It wasn't true for Mr. Agani at the time too. Mr. Agani was killed a month later. Whereas, I left Kosova in hiding, I left in disguise. I left the basement. I moved in disguise, not as Baton Haxhiu. I tried to go into houses under this disguise and ask for shelter, but nobody would take me in. When I would knock at someone's door and tell people I'm Baton Haxhiu, they would just say to me, How dare you, you should be ashamed of yourself, he is dead. It was a very difficult period. These two days were very difficult for me. Nobody believed me. They didn't believe I was alive. They believed more in the NATO statement than they believed me, whom they saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: As a journalist, you are familiar with investigative practices. Did you ever approach NATO to ask them what the source of their misinformation was?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Precisely. That list that NATO got from its sources, the list of people that had to be executed, this list was in the possession of Mr. Sainovic. That's what we learned later. The list of so-called enemies. Many of the people whose names appeared on that list were killed, even Mr. Surroi, Alush Gashi, myself, and some others were announced dead, although we were still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Have you seen this list yourself?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I cannot give you an answer for that. I don't have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I know, but is have you seen it, a copy of it?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I already told you, I don't have an answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: My last question is, on what basis do you claim that this list was in the possession of Mr. Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: Ten years have passed since the war in Kosova. I investigated my personal circumstances under which I was announced dead. I asked family members, friends about the circumstances of Mr. Welby and Mr. Shea declaring me dead. I asked Mr. Shea in person about this. I asked other UK diplomats about this. That's why I'm telling you I'm familiar with what that list was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understand. But my question is who told you that Mr. Sainovic had possession of that list, at the time?

utterances.speaker: BATON HAXHIU
utterances.text: I told you, I don't have an answer to that, and I'm not going to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiu, you'll be pleased to know that that concludes the questions for you. We have managed it in the time. We would like to thank you for your attendance here, for the assistance that you've given, and for the interest in the discussion between yourself and counsel. You are, of course, now free to go back to your normal activities. We must now adjourn for the day. We thank you again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 19th day of June, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.
